source.title: High-dimensional dynamics of generalization error in neural networks
source.authors: Madhu S. Advani; Andrew M. Saxe; H. Sompolinsky

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses student–teacher simulations and analytical training dynamics rather than reproducing the original image-label randomization experiments. Its nonlinear simulations test fitting nearly random targets; its analytical results address how output noise affects training error and time.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results in Sections 2.6 and 5. Figure 9 tests nearly random and nearly noise-free targets, with the nonlinear network setting described as the same as Figure 6. The text does not give numerical values for the plotted errors. Results attributed to Zhang et al. (2017) and Arpit et al. (2017) are prior work and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Figure 9 directly tests memorization of nearly random targets using nonlinear ReLU networks and Gaussian inputs. This is a student–teacher regression analogue of V1 and the Gaussian-input part of V3, using a fixed first layer and batch gradient descent.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for Section 5. More broadly, the authors conclude that very large networks can reduce overtraining and improve generalization, provided initialization weights are small. Their explanation combines a frozen subspace with an increasing nonzero eigengap; early stopping is especially useful outside the high-SNR, strongly overcomplete regime.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a student–teacher setup with Gaussian inputs and noisy outputs, including nonlinear ReLU students with fixed or trained layers; it does not reproduce the original image-label randomization recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Target SNR changes the outcome: nearly random targets (SNR = 0.01) are fit but generalize poorly, while nearly noise-free targets (SNR = 10) generalize well. Model size and early stopping also affect the reported behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: At high SNR, the largest fixed-first-layer ReLU network generalizes best even without early stopping.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sufficiently wide networks initialized with small weights can generalize well on strong teacher-generated signal without early stopping.

fits_no_version.finding: For an undersampled shallow linear regressor, time to a fixed small training error grows logarithmically with output-noise variance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient descent can memorize noisier regression targets with only logarithmically increasing training time in an undersampled linear model.

record.problems: Figure 9 provides no numerical error values in the text. The random-target test uses a student–teacher setup and nearly random targets rather than random labels on images; the paper does not state that test error is at chance. The analytical training-time result concerns shallow linear networks and is not a direct test of the V2 deep-network comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result rows were omitted. Figure 9's plotted numerical values are not reconstructed because the text does not state them.

untested.parts: Completely randomized class labels, chance-level test error, and standard deep networks trained with stochastic gradient methods. Figure 9 compares target SNR using the same model family, but does not establish the full architecture-and-hyperparameter claim.
The small constant-factor comparison in standard deep networks and convergence as a function of the fraction of corrupted labels.
Shuffled pixels and independently permuted pixels; transfer of the Gaussian-input result to the original deep architectures and training procedures.
A sweep from no corrupted labels to completely corrupted labels, with perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error.
Effects of weight decay, dropout and augmentation on random-label fitting, and controlled removal of these regularizers on true-label generalization.
Direct measurement of shared real-data patterns being learned before noisy labels. Eigenmode dynamics and early-stopping benefits do not separately measure those two learning processes.

record.verdict_notes: Missing measurement of chance performance is an untested part of V1, not a limits_scope result. Likewise, the shallow linear analysis does not justify a limits_scope verdict on deep-network optimization. Figure 9's caption supplies the reliable panel mapping: A–B low SNR, C–D high SNR.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests nearly random target labels in its student–teacher setting, not a completely random labeling of training images in the original settings. It does not report test error explicitly at chance or test the same architecture and training hyperparameters as the original studies.

The paper derives a logarithmic increase in time to reach a specified small training error as output noise increases, for an undersampled linear student–teacher setting. It does not test the stated small constant-factor comparison in standard deep networks or sweep the fraction of corrupted labels.
The paper does not test shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
The paper does not sweep the fraction of randomly corrupted labels from none to all, or report steadily rising test error across such a sweep.

The paper discusses early stopping and L2 regularization, but does not test weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation against random-label fitting or their removal against true-label generalization.
The paper does not measure the order in which true-label patterns and noisy or random labels are learned over training.

rows.note: The text says the low-SNR networks do not generalize well; it does not state that their test error is at chance.
rows.check: Poor regression generalization does not establish chance-level classification performance. The qualitative statement applies to the low-SNR overcomplete networks collectively, rather than exclusively to Nh = 16326. It does not demonstrate incomplete memorization.

rows.subject: nonlinear ReLU networks with fixed first layer (same setting as Fig 6)
rows.operation_detail: Trained on nearly noise-free target labels (SNR = 10).
rows.value: attains the best generalization performance of all models in the high-SNR regime
rows.note: The authors describe the targets as nearly noise-free and say the same model sizes generalize well; no numerical test error is stated.
rows.check: Good generalization on high-SNR teacher targets does not measure random-label fitting. It also lacks the removal or comparison of explicit regularizers required to establish V5.

rows.subject: shallow linear student network
rows.operation_detail: Derived training-error dynamics for noisy outputs and estimated time to reach training error proportional to δ.
rows.measure: Training time to reach the specified training error
rows.value: time scales logarithmically with increased output noise variance
rows.note: This is an analytical result in a shallow linear setting, not a measured constant-factor comparison in standard deep networks; the paper does not vary a fraction of corrupted labels.
rows.check: The logarithmic training-time result is correctly extracted, but concerns a shallow linear regressor under continuous-time batch gradient descent. It does not measure V2's training-time comparison in standard deep networks or its corrupted-label-fraction dependence.
